Explanation: 6n means 6 × n. Undo it: 60 ÷ 6 = 10.

Subject: maths
Question or text: 7n + 10 = 59. What is n?
Explanation: Subtract 10: 7n = 49. Divide by 7: n = 7.

Subject: maths
Question or text: 9n + 15 = 69. What is n?
Explanation: Subtract 15: 9n = 54. Divide by 9: n = 6.

Subject: maths
Question or text: 6n + 9 = 81. What is n?
Explanation: Subtract 9: 6n = 72. Divide by 6: n = 12.

Subject: maths
Item: algebra:Tickets cost C = 7n + 2 pounds for n people. What is C when n = 7?
Question or text: Tickets cost C = 7n + 2 pounds for n people. What is C when n = 7?

Subject: maths
Item: algebra:Tickets cost C = 4n + 7 pounds for n people. What is C when n = 8?
Question or text: Tickets cost C = 4n + 7 pounds for n people. What is C when n = 8?

Subject: maths
Item: algebra:Tickets cost C = 7n + 5 pounds for n people. What is C when n = 10?
Question or text: Tickets cost C = 7n + 5 pounds for n people. What is C when n = 10?

Subject: maths
Question or text: 6n − 31 = 35. What is n?
Explanation: Add 31: 6n = 66. Divide by 6: n = 11.

Subject: maths
Item: algebra:A sequence goes 17, 21, 25, 29, … What is the 20th term?
Question or text: A sequence goes 17, 21, 25, 29, … What is the 20th term?
Explanation: It goes up by 4 each time. The 20th term is 19 steps after the first: 17 + 19 × 4 = 93.

Subject: maths
Item: algebra:A sequence goes 18, 20, 22, 24, … What is the 20th term?
Question or text: A sequence goes 18, 20, 22, 24, … What is the 20th term?
Explanation: It goes up by 2 each time. The 20th term is 19 steps after the first: 18 + 19 × 2 = 56.

Subject: maths
Item: geometry-statistics:Two angles sit on a straight line. One is 62°. What is the other, in degrees?
Question or text: Two angles sit on a straight line. One is 62°. What is the other, in degrees?
Explanation: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°: 180 − 62 = 118°.

Subject: maths
Item: geometry-statistics:Two angles sit on a straight line. One is 89°. What is the other, in degrees?
Question or text: Two angles sit on a straight line. One is 89°. What is the other, in degrees?
Explanation: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°: 180 − 89 = 91°.

Subject: maths
Item: geometry-statistics:Two angles sit on a straight line. One is 98°. What is the other, in degrees?
Question or text: Two angles sit on a straight line. One is 98°. What is the other, in degrees?
Explanation: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°: 180 − 98 = 82°.

Subject: maths
Item: geometry-statistics:A triangle has angles of 87° and 55°. What is the third angle, in degrees?
Question or text: A triangle has angles of 87° and 55°. What is the third angle, in degrees?
Explanation: Angles in a triangle add up to 180°: 180 − 87 − 55 = 38°.

Subject: maths
Item: geometry-statistics:A triangle has angles of 22° and 123°. What is the third angle, in degrees?
Question or text: A triangle has angles of 22° and 123°. What is the third angle, in degrees?
Explanation: Angles in a triangle add up to 180°: 180 − 22 − 123 = 35°.

Subject: maths
Item: geometry-statistics:A triangle has angles of 94° and 36°. What is the third angle, in degrees?
Question or text: A triangle has angles of 94° and 36°. What is the third angle, in degrees?
Explanation: Angles in a triangle add up to 180°: 180 − 94 − 36 = 50°.

Subject: maths
Item: geometry-statistics:A triangle has a base of 8 cm and a perpendicular height of 5 cm. What is its area in cm²?
Question or text: A triangle has a base of 8 cm and a perpendicular height of 5 cm. What is its area in cm²?
Explanation: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height = ½ × 8 × 5 = 20 cm².

Subject: maths
Item: geometry-statistics:A triangle has a base of 16 cm and a perpendicular height of 17 cm. What is its area in cm²?
Question or text: A triangle has a base of 16 cm and a perpendicular height of 17 cm. What is its area in cm²?
Explanation: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height = ½ × 16 × 17 = 136 cm².

Subject: maths
Item: geometry-statistics:A circle has a radius of 13 cm. What is its diameter, in cm?
Question or text: A circle has a radius of 13 cm. What is its diameter, in cm?
Explanation: The diameter is twice the radius: 2 × 13 = 26 cm.

Subject: maths
Item: geometry-statistics:A parallelogram has a base of 3 cm and a perpendicular height of 3 cm. What is its area in cm²?
Question or text: A parallelogram has a base of 3 cm and a perpendicular height of 3 cm. What is its area in cm²?
Explanation: Area of a parallelogram = base × height = 3 × 3 = 9 cm².

Subject: maths
Item: geometry-statistics:A parallelogram has a base of 14 cm and a perpendicular height of 3 cm. What is its area in cm²?
Question or text: A parallelogram has a base of 14 cm and a perpendicular height of 3 cm. What is its area in cm²?
Explanation: Area of a parallelogram = base × height = 14 × 3 = 42 cm².

Subject: maths
Question or text: What is the mean of 7, 15, 9, 25?
Explanation: Add them up: 7 + 15 + 9 + 25 = 56. Divide by how many there are (4): 56 ÷ 4 = 14.

Subject: maths
Item: geometry-statistics:A quadrilateral has angles of 124°, 100° and 74°. What is the fourth angle, in degrees?
Question or text: A quadrilateral has angles of 124°, 100° and 74°. What is the fourth angle, in degrees?
Explanation: Angles in a quadrilateral add up to 360°: 360 − 124 − 100 − 74 = 62°.

Subject: maths
Question or text: What is the mean of 36, 32, 35, 27, 110?
Explanation: Add them up: 36 + 32 + 35 + 27 + 110 = 240. Divide by how many there are (5): 240 ÷ 5 = 48.

Subject: maths
Item: geometry-statistics:What is the size of each interior angle of a regular dodecagon (12 sides), in degrees?
Question or text: What is the size of each interior angle of a regular dodecagon (12 sides), in degrees?
Explanation: The interior angles of a 12-sided shape add up to (12 − 2) × 180 = 1800°. Shared equally: 1800 ÷ 12 = 150°.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which of these is a living thing?
Choices: A tree | A rock | A cloud | A chair
Explanation: Trees grow, need water and food, and make new trees. Rocks, clouds and chairs do not.

Subject: science
Question or text: What is a baby frog called?
Choices: A tadpole | A puppy | A calf | A chick
Explanation: Frogs hatch from eggs as tadpoles, which live in water and slowly grow legs.

Subject: science
Question or text: Along with water and air, what do plants need to make their food?
Explanation: Plants use energy from sunlight to make their own food.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
Choices: The roots | The petals | The flowers | The seeds
Explanation: Roots grow into the soil and soak up water and minerals.

Subject: science
Question or text: An animal that eats only plants is called a…
Explanation: Herbivores (like rabbits and cows) eat plants. Carnivores eat meat; omnivores eat both.

Subject: science
Question or text: What do fish use to breathe underwater?
Explanation: Gills take oxygen out of the water as it flows over them.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which of these animals is a mammal?
Choices: A whale | A shark | A salmon | An octopus
Explanation: Whales breathe air with lungs and feed their babies milk, so they are mammals, not fish.

Subject: science
Question or text: A caterpillar grows up to become a…
Choices: Butterfly or moth | Beetle | Spider | Worm
Explanation: Caterpillars are the young (larva) stage of butterflies and moths.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which gas do plants take in from the air to make food?
Explanation: Plants take in carbon dioxide and, using sunlight and water, turn it into sugar.

Subject: science
Question or text: What is the process called where plants make food using sunlight?
Explanation: "Photo" means light and "synthesis" means making: plants make food with light.

Subject: science
Question or text: In the food chain grass → rabbit → fox, which one is the producer?
Choices: Grass | Rabbit | Fox | None of them
Explanation: Producers make their own food from sunlight. Plants are producers; animals are consumers.

Subject: science
Question or text: Animals without a backbone are called…
Explanation: Insects, worms, spiders and snails have no backbone, so they are invertebrates.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which gas do plants give off during photosynthesis?
Explanation: Photosynthesis releases oxygen, which animals (and people) need to breathe.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which part of a plant cell contains the green chlorophyll?
Explanation: Chloroplasts hold chlorophyll, which captures light energy for photosynthesis.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which sense do you use your nose for?
Explanation: Your nose detects smells. Ears hear, eyes see and skin feels touch.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which organ pumps blood around your body?
Choices: The heart | The lungs | The stomach | The brain
Explanation: The heart is a strong muscle that pumps blood all day and night.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which organs do you use to breathe?
Choices: The lungs | The kidneys | The heart | The liver
Explanation: Your lungs fill with air and take oxygen into your blood.

Subject: science
Question or text: What protects your brain?
Choices: The skull | The ribs | The spine | The kneecap
Explanation: The skull is a hard case of bone around the brain.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which part of your body helps you taste food?
Choices: The tongue | The elbow | The ear | The hair
Explanation: Taste buds on your tongue detect flavours like sweet, salty and sour.

Subject: science
Question or text: About how many bones does an adult human have?
Explanation: Babies are born with more bones, but some join together, leaving about 206 in adults.

Subject: science
Question or text: What do your muscles pull on so that you can move?
Explanation: Muscles are attached to bones and pull on them to move your body.

Subject: science
Question or text: Where does food go right after you swallow it?
Choices: The food pipe (oesophagus) | The lungs | The heart | The kidneys
Explanation: The oesophagus carries food from your mouth down to your stomach.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which organs clean your blood and make urine?
Choices: The kidneys | The lungs | The heart | The stomach
Explanation: Kidneys filter waste out of the blood and turn it into urine.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which blood cells help fight germs?
Choices: White blood cells | Red blood cells | Platelets | Nerve cells
Explanation: White blood cells are part of your immune system and attack germs.

Subject: science
Question or text: What is the largest organ of the human body?
Choices: The skin | The liver | The brain | The lungs
Explanation: Skin covers your whole body, making it the largest organ.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
Explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins bring it back.

Subject: science
Question or text: Where are most nutrients from food absorbed into the blood?
Choices: The small intestine | The stomach | The large intestine | The mouth
Explanation: The small intestine is long and lined with tiny finger-like villi that absorb nutrients.

Subject: science
Question or text: What is the longest bone in the human body?
Choices: The femur (thigh bone) | The spine | The skull | The humerus (upper arm)
Explanation: The femur runs from your hip to your knee.

Subject: science
Question or text: Ice is water in which state?
Explanation: Ice keeps its own shape, so it is a solid.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which material can you see through?
Explanation: Clear glass is transparent, so light passes through it.

Subject: science
Question or text: What happens to ice when it warms up?
Choices: It melts into water | It turns into sand | It gets bigger | Nothing happens
Explanation: Heat makes ice melt from a solid into liquid water.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which material would be best for a raincoat?
Explanation: Plastic is waterproof, so rain cannot soak through it.

Subject: science
Question or text: Steam is water as a…
Explanation: When water boils it turns into a gas called steam (water vapour).

Subject: science
Question or text: At what temperature does pure water freeze?
Explanation: Pure water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C (at sea level).

Subject: science
Question or text: At what temperature does pure water boil at sea level?
Explanation: At sea level, pure water boils at 100 °C.

Subject: science
Question or text: When water vapour cools and turns back into liquid, it is called…
Explanation: That is why drops form on a cold glass: water vapour in the air condenses.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which of these conducts electricity well?
Explanation: Copper is a metal and a good conductor, which is why it is used in wires.

Subject: science
Question or text: When a liquid slowly turns into a gas, it is called…
Explanation: Puddles dry up because the water evaporates into the air.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which of these is a natural material?
Explanation: Wool comes from sheep. Plastic, nylon and polyester are made by people.

Subject: science
Question or text: In which state are particles held in fixed places, only vibrating?
Choices: Solid | Liquid | Gas | They are the same in all states
Explanation: In a solid, particles are held in place and only vibrate, so it keeps its shape. In liquids and gases they move around.

Subject: science
Question or text: When sugar dissolves completely in water, the mixture is called a…
Explanation: A solution forms when one substance dissolves evenly into another.

Subject: science
Question or text: Everything around us is made of tiny particles called…
Explanation: Atoms are the tiny building blocks of all matter.

Subject: science
Question or text: A push or a pull is called a…
Explanation: Every push or pull is a force. Forces can make things move, stop or change shape.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which of these will a magnet pick up?
Choices: An iron paperclip | A plastic spoon | A wooden pencil | A paper cup
Explanation: Magnets attract iron and steel, but not plastic, wood or paper.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which force pulls things down towards the Earth?
Explanation: Gravity is why things fall when you drop them.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which of these gives off its own light?
Choices: The Sun | The Moon | A mirror | A window
Explanation: The Sun makes its own light. The Moon and mirrors only reflect light.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which force slows down a ball rolling on grass?
Explanation: Friction happens when surfaces rub together, and it slows moving things down.

Subject: science
Question or text: What happens when you put the north poles of two magnets together?
Choices: They push apart | They stick together | Nothing happens | They get hot
Explanation: Like poles repel (push apart); opposite poles attract.

Subject: science
Question or text: How is a shadow made?
Choices: An object blocks light | Light bounces off water | The ground gets darker by itself | Wind blows light away
Explanation: Light travels in straight lines, so an object in the way leaves a dark shape behind it.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which surface gives the most friction?
Choices: Sandpaper | Ice | Glass | A polished floor
Explanation: Rough surfaces like sandpaper grip more, which means more friction.

Subject: science
Question or text: What does a switch do in an electric circuit?
Choices: Opens or closes the circuit | Makes electricity | Stores the battery | Changes the bulb colour
Explanation: When a switch is off, it makes a gap, so electricity cannot flow around the circuit.

Subject: science
Question or text: What causes sound?
Explanation: Sound is made when something vibrates, like a guitar string or your vocal cords.

Subject: science
Question or text: What kind of energy does a moving car have?
Choices: Kinetic energy | Sound energy only | Light energy only | No energy
Explanation: Anything that moves has kinetic energy (energy of motion).

Subject: science
Question or text: Which travels faster?
Choices: Light | Sound | They travel at the same speed | It depends on the colour
Explanation: Light is far faster than sound, which is why you see lightning before you hear thunder.

Subject: science
Question or text: A solar panel changes light energy into…
Choices: Electrical energy | Sound energy | Chemical energy in food | Magnetism
Explanation: Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity.

Subject: science
Question or text: What is the unit used to measure force?
Choices: The newton | The metre | The litre | The gram
Explanation: Force is measured in newtons (N), named after Isaac Newton.

Subject: science
Question or text: What is the name of the star at the centre of our solar system?
Choices: The Sun | The Moon | Mars | The North Star
Explanation: The Sun is a star, and all the planets in our solar system travel around it.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which planet do we live on?
Explanation: We live on Earth, the third planet from the Sun.

Subject: science
Question or text: About how long does Earth take to travel once around the Sun?
Choices: One year | One day | One week | One month
Explanation: Earth takes about 365 days, one year, to orbit the Sun.

Subject: science
Question or text: About how long does Earth take to spin around once?
Choices: One day (24 hours) | One hour | One week | One year
Explanation: One full spin of Earth takes about 24 hours, giving us one day.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
Explanation: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun.

Subject: science
Question or text: What causes day and night?
Choices: Earth spinning on its axis | The Sun going around Earth | The Moon blocking the Sun | Clouds covering the Sun
Explanation: As Earth spins, your side faces the Sun (day) and then turns away (night).

Subject: science
Question or text: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
Explanation: Mars looks red because of iron-rich dust (rust) on its surface.

Subject: science
Question or text: What is the largest planet in our solar system?
Explanation: Jupiter is a giant gas planet with more mass than all the other planets put together.

Subject: science
Question or text: How many planets are in our solar system?
Explanation: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Pluto is now called a dwarf planet.

Subject: science
Question or text: Rain, snow, sleet and hail are all kinds of…
Explanation: Precipitation is any water that falls from clouds to the ground.

Subject: science
Question or text: What causes Earth to have seasons?
Choices: The tilt of Earth's axis | Earth getting closer to and further from the Sun | The Moon changing shape | Clouds blocking the Sun
Explanation: Earth is tilted, so each half gets more direct sunlight for part of the year (summer).

Subject: science
Question or text: Why does the Moon shine at night?
Choices: It reflects light from the Sun | It makes its own light | It is on fire | It reflects light from Earth’s cities
Correct answer: It reflects light from the Sun
Explanation: The Moon has no light of its own; we see sunlight bouncing off it.

Subject: science
Question or text: In the water cycle, how do clouds form?
Choices: Water vapour cools and condenses | Wind blows dust together | The Sun makes smoke | Rain goes back up
Explanation: Warm water vapour rises, cools and condenses into tiny droplets that make clouds.

Subject: science
Question or text: Animals with a backbone are called…
Explanation: Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals all have a backbone, so they are vertebrates.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which of these is an invertebrate?
Choices: A snail | A frog | A robin | A salmon
Explanation: A snail has no backbone. Frogs, robins and salmon are vertebrates.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which group of vertebrates has feathers?
Explanation: Only birds have feathers.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which vertebrate group has dry, scaly skin?
Explanation: Reptiles such as lizards and snakes have dry, scaly skin. Amphibians have moist skin.

Subject: science
Question or text: How many legs does an insect have?
Explanation: All adult insects have 6 legs and 3 body parts.

Subject: science
Question or text: Why is a spider not an insect?
Choices: It has eight legs | It has wings | It has a backbone | It has six legs
Explanation: Spiders have 8 legs and 2 body parts. Insects have 6 legs and 3 body parts.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which of these is a micro-organism?
Choices: Bacteria | A mushroom | A worm | An ant
Explanation: Micro-organisms are too small to see without a microscope. Bacteria are micro-organisms.

Subject: science
Question or text: Frogs and other amphibians usually…
Choices: Live in water when young and on land as adults | Live only in the sea | Have feathers | Feed their young on milk
Correct answer: Live in water when young and on land as adults
Explanation: Frogs start as tadpoles in water, then grow lungs and legs and can live on land.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which scientist was a pioneer of classification and gave living things two-part Latin names?
Choices: Carl Linnaeus | Charles Darwin | Isaac Newton | Mary Anning
Explanation: Carl Linnaeus created the naming system we still use, such as Homo sapiens for humans.

Subject: science
Question or text: What is a classification key used for?
Choices: Identifying a living thing by answering questions about its features | Unlocking a science lab | Measuring how heavy an animal is | Counting how many animals live in a place
Correct answer: Identifying a living thing by answering questions about its features
Explanation: A key asks yes/no questions about features (such as "Does it have legs?") to work out what something is.

Subject: science
Question or text: A whale and a bat are both…
Explanation: Both breathe air, have hair and feed their babies milk, so both are mammals.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which feature do ALL mammals share?
Choices: They feed their young on milk | They give birth to live young | They live on land | They have four legs
Correct answer: They feed their young on milk
Explanation: All mammals feed their young on milk. A few, like the platypus, lay eggs, so "live young" is not true of every mammal.

Subject: science
Question or text: The mould that grows on old bread is a type of…
Explanation: Moulds, yeasts and mushrooms are fungi.

Subject: science
Question or text: Why are fungi, like mushrooms, not classified as plants?
Choices: They cannot make their own food by photosynthesis | They are always poisonous | They only grow at night | They are not made of cells
Correct answer: They cannot make their own food by photosynthesis
Explanation: Plants make food using sunlight. Fungi cannot, so they feed on other things, like dead leaves.

Subject: science
Question or text: What is the main job of the heart?
Choices: To pump blood around the body | To digest food | To help us think | To store air
Correct answer: To pump blood around the body
Explanation: The heart is a muscle that pumps blood through blood vessels to every part of the body.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which of these helps keep your heart healthy?
Choices: Regular exercise | Smoking | Sitting still all day | Eating lots of sweets
Explanation: Exercise makes the heart muscle stronger. Smoking and too much sugar and fat can harm it.

Subject: science
Question or text: Blood vessels that carry blood back to the heart are called…
Explanation: Veins carry blood back to the heart. Arteries carry it away from the heart.

Subject: science
Question or text: What does blood carry to every part of the body?
Choices: Oxygen and nutrients | Only water | Bones | Air bubbles
Explanation: Blood delivers oxygen from the lungs and nutrients from food, and carries away waste.

Subject: science
Question or text: The tiniest blood vessels are called…
Explanation: Capillaries are so thin that oxygen and nutrients can pass through their walls into the body.

Subject: science
Question or text: Where does blood pick up oxygen?
Choices: In the lungs | In the stomach | In the kidneys | In the brain
Explanation: Oxygen from the air we breathe passes into the blood in the lungs.

Subject: science
Question or text: Why does your heart beat faster when you exercise?
Choices: Your muscles need more oxygen | Your bones are growing | You are digesting food | Your blood is getting colder
Explanation: Working muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps faster to deliver it.

Subject: science
Question or text: How many chambers does the human heart have?
Explanation: The heart has 4 chambers: two atria at the top and two ventricles at the bottom.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which part of the blood helps it clot when you cut yourself?
Choices: Platelets | Red blood cells | Plasma | White blood cells
Explanation: Platelets stick together to plug a cut and stop the bleeding.

Subject: science
Question or text: The liquid part of blood, which carries dissolved nutrients, is called…
Explanation: Plasma is mostly water and carries nutrients, water and waste around the body.

Subject: science
Question or text: Smoking is especially harmful to which organs?
Choices: The heart and lungs | The hair and nails | The teeth only | The bones only
Explanation: Smoking damages the lungs and blood vessels and makes heart disease more likely.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs?
Choices: The right side | The left side | Neither side | The heart does not pump blood to the lungs
Explanation: The right side pumps blood to the lungs to collect oxygen. The left side pumps it to the rest of the body.

Subject: science
Question or text: Why do arteries have thicker walls than veins?
Choices: They carry blood at high pressure straight from the heart | They carry more oxygen | They are older | They carry food instead of blood
Correct answer: They carry blood at high pressure straight from the heart
Explanation: Each heartbeat pushes blood into the arteries at high pressure, so they need thick, stretchy walls.

Subject: science
Question or text: How are nutrients from digested food carried around the body?
Choices: Dissolved in the blood | Along the nerves | Through the bones | In the air we breathe
Explanation: Nutrients pass from the small intestine into the blood, which carries them to every cell.

Subject: science
Question or text: What is a fossil?
Choices: The remains or traces of a living thing from long ago, preserved in rock | A type of crystal | A plant that is still growing | A rock shaped by the sea
Correct answer: The remains or traces of a living thing from long ago, preserved in rock
Explanation: Fossils form over millions of years, often when a plant or animal is buried and turned to rock.

Subject: science
Question or text: What are the offspring of a living thing?
Choices: Its young | Its parents | Its food | Its home
Explanation: Offspring are the young that a plant or animal produces.

Subject: science
Question or text: Are offspring usually identical to their parents?
Choices: No, they are similar but usually vary | Yes, always exactly the same | No, they look nothing alike | Only in plants
Correct answer: No, they are similar but usually vary
Explanation: Offspring are the same kind of living thing as their parents but are not identical. This is called variation.

Subject: science
Question or text: An arctic fox has thick white fur. This helps it survive in the snow and is an example of…
Explanation: An adaptation is a feature that helps a living thing survive in its environment.

Subject: science
Question or text: How does a camel's hump help it survive in the desert?
Choices: It stores fat that can be used for energy | It stores water | It keeps the camel cool | It helps the camel see further
Correct answer: It stores fat that can be used for energy
Explanation: A camel's hump stores fat, not water. The fat can be used for energy when food is scarce.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which fossil hunter made famous discoveries at Lyme Regis?
Choices: Mary Anning | Carl Linnaeus | Isaac Newton | Florence Nightingale
Explanation: Mary Anning found ichthyosaur and plesiosaur fossils on the Dorset coast in the early 1800s.

Subject: science
Question or text: How are cactuses adapted to hot deserts?
Choices: They store water in thick stems and have spines instead of broad leaves | They grow huge soft leaves | They need lots of rain every day | They only grow in shade
Correct answer: They store water in thick stems and have spines instead of broad leaves
Explanation: Thick stems store water, and spines lose less water than broad leaves (and protect the plant).

Subject: science
Question or text: Features passed from parents to their offspring are…
Choices: Inherited | Learnt at school | Caught like a cold | Made up
Explanation: Inherited characteristics, like eye colour, are passed on from parents.

Subject: science
Question or text: Which two scientists developed the idea of evolution by natural selection?
Choices: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace | Isaac Newton and Albert Einstein | Mary Anning and Carl Linnaeus | Marie Curie and Louis Pasteur
Correct answer: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace
Explanation: Darwin and Wallace both came up with natural selection, and their ideas were presented together in 1858.

Subject: science
Question or text: In natural selection, which living things are most likely to survive and have offspring?
Choices: Those best adapted to their environment | Always the biggest ones | Always the oldest ones | Those that move the least
Correct answer: Those best adapted to their environment
Explanation: Living things with helpful features survive better, so they have more offspring and pass those features on.

Subject: science
Question or text: If a labrador and a poodle have puppies, the puppies will…
Choices: Have a mix of features from both parents | Look exactly like the poodle | Not be dogs | Have no features from either parent
Correct answer: Have a mix of features from both parents
Explanation: Offspring inherit characteristics from both parents, so they show a mix.

Subject: science
Question or text: What do fossils tell us about living things?
Choices: They have changed over millions of years | They never change | Dinosaurs are alive today | All animals lived at the same time
Correct answer: They have changed over millions of years
Explanation: Fossils show animals and plants that no longer exist, and how living things have changed over time.

Subject: science
Question or text: According to natural selection, why do giraffes have long necks?
Choices: Giraffes born with longer necks reached more food, survived, and passed long necks on | Giraffes stretched their necks and passed the stretch on to their babies | Giraffes decided to grow longer necks | Their necks grew because they ate leaves
Correct answer: Giraffes born with longer necks reached more food, survived, and passed long necks on
Explanation: Stretching during life is not passed on. Natural variation plus survival of the best adapted explains it.

Subject: science
Question or text: Why is variation between offspring important for evolution?
Choices: Some variations help survival, and these get passed on | It makes all animals identical | It stops animals from changing | It only affects plants
Correct answer: Some variations help survival, and these get passed on
Explanation: Without variation there would be nothing for natural selection to choose between.

Subject: science

Explanation: Light travels in straight lines, which is why it cannot go around objects.

Explanation: A light source gives out its own light. Mirrors, the Moon and walls only reflect light.

Subject: science

Choices: Light reflects off the book into our eyes | Light shines out of our eyes onto the book | The book makes its own light | We can see without any light
Correct answer: Light reflects off the book into our eyes
Explanation: Light travels from a source, bounces off the book, and travels in a straight line into our eyes.

Subject: science

Choices: Light travels in straight lines, so the object blocks light in its own shape | Shadows are copies made by our eyes | The object gives out dark light | Light bends around the object
Correct answer: Light travels in straight lines, so the object blocks light in its own shape
Explanation: The object blocks the straight-line light rays, leaving a dark area with the same outline.

Subject: science
Question or text: What happens to a shadow when you move an object closer to the light source?
Choices: It gets bigger | It gets smaller | It stays the same size | It disappears
Explanation: Closer to the light, the object blocks more of the spreading light, so the shadow grows.

Subject: science

Choices: A mirror | Black paper | A carpet | A wooden table
Explanation: Smooth, shiny surfaces like mirrors reflect light best.

Subject: science

Choices: Two mirrors | A magnet | A torch | A shadow
Explanation: Light reflects off the top mirror, down to the bottom mirror and into your eye.

Subject: science
Question or text: Why should you never look directly at the Sun?
Choices: Its light is so strong it can damage your eyes | It will make the Sun go out | It makes shadows disappear | The Sun is too far away to see
Correct answer: Its light is so strong it can damage your eyes
Explanation: Sunlight is very intense and can permanently damage your eyes, even through sunglasses.

Subject: science

Explanation: Opaque materials block all light, so they make the darkest shadows.

Choices: Changes direction as it passes between water and air | Is blocked by the water | Is soaked up by the straw | Stops travelling in water
Correct answer: Changes direction as it passes between water and air
Explanation: Light bends when it moves from one material to another. This is called refraction.

Subject: science

Correct answer: Is split into colours by raindrops
Explanation: Raindrops bend and split white sunlight into its colours.

Subject: science

Correct answer: A mixture of all the colours
Explanation: A prism or raindrops can split white light into red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.

Subject: science

Choices: It reflects red light and absorbs most other colours | It gives out red light | It absorbs red light | Red light cannot reach it
Correct answer: It reflects red light and absorbs most other colours
Explanation: We see the colour of light that an object reflects into our eyes.

Explanation: Electricity can only flow if there is a complete loop from the cell, through the bulb and back.

Subject: science
Question or text: What does a cell (battery) do in a circuit?

Explanation: The cell is the power source that pushes the current around the circuit.

Subject: science
Question or text: In a series circuit, what happens to a bulb if you add another cell?
Choices: It gets brighter | It gets dimmer | Nothing changes | It changes colour
Explanation: More cells give a higher voltage, so more energy reaches the bulb and it glows brighter.

Subject: science

Choices: It gets louder | It gets quieter | It stops working | Nothing changes
Explanation: A higher voltage gives the buzzer more energy, so it sounds louder.

Subject: science
Question or text: What happens when a switch is open (off)?
Choices: The circuit is broken and electricity stops flowing | The bulb gets brighter | The cell recharges | Electricity flows faster
Correct answer: The circuit is broken and electricity stops flowing
Explanation: An open switch makes a gap in the circuit.

Subject: science
Question or text: In a series circuit with one cell, what happens if you add a second bulb?
Choices: Both bulbs are dimmer | Both bulbs are brighter | Nothing changes | One bulb goes out
Explanation: The same cell now has to push electricity through two bulbs, so each gets less energy and is dimmer.

Subject: science

Explanation: Voltage is measured in volts (V). A typical AA cell is 1.5 V.

Explanation: Metals like steel conduct electricity. Plastic, rubber and wood are insulators.

Subject: science

Explanation: A circle with a cross is the symbol for a lamp (bulb).

Subject: science

Choices: A cell | A bulb | A wire | A motor
Explanation: The cell symbol is a long line (positive) next to a short line (negative).

Subject: science
Question or text: Why do scientists use symbols in circuit diagrams?
Choices: They are simple and understood everywhere | They look prettier than drawings | They make circuits work better | They are secret codes
Correct answer: They are simple and understood everywhere
Explanation: Standard symbols make circuits quick to draw and easy for anyone to read.

Subject: science
Question or text: If one bulb breaks in a series circuit, what happens to the other bulbs?
Choices: They go out too | They get brighter | They stay the same | They change colour
Explanation: A series circuit is a single loop. One broken bulb breaks the loop for everything.

Subject: science
Question or text: Why might a bulb blow if you connect too many cells?
Choices: The voltage is too high for the bulb | The wires get too long | The cells run out | The switch is off
Correct answer: The voltage is too high for the bulb
Explanation: Each bulb is made for a certain voltage. Too high and its thin filament overheats and breaks.

Subject: science

Explanation: A motor uses electricity to make something spin.

Explanation: A draft is a first attempt at writing something.

Subject: english
Question or text: The car was ___ at the traffic lights.
Explanation: Stationary means not moving. Stationery (e for envelopes) is paper, pens and so on.

Subject: english
Question or text: Pens, paper and envelopes are called ___.
Explanation: Stationery: remember "e for envelopes".

Subject: english
Question or text: After the long walk we felt ___.
Explanation: Weary means tired. Wary means cautious.

Subject: english
Question or text: Be ___ of strangers you meet online.
Explanation: Wary means cautious. Weary means tired.

Subject: english
Question or text: The cold weather may ___ our plans.
Explanation: Affect is usually a verb. Effect is usually a noun.

Subject: english
Question or text: The medicine had a good ___.
Explanation: Effect is usually a noun: an effect.

Subject: english
Question or text: Honesty is an important ___.
Explanation: A principle is a basic truth or belief.

Subject: english
Question or text: The ___ of the college gave a speech.
Explanation: A principal is the most important person, such as the head of a college.

Subject: english
Question or text: She paid me a lovely ___ about my drawing.
Explanation: A compliment is a nice remark.

Subject: english
Question or text: The red scarf is the perfect ___ to her coat.
Explanation: A complement completes something (think "complete").

Subject: english
Question or text: My uncle has a driving ___.
Explanation: In British English, licence (with c) is the noun.

Subject: english
Question or text: The council will ___ the café to sell food.
Explanation: In British English, license (with s) is the verb.

Subject: english
Question or text: Please ___ to the exit.
Explanation: Proceed means go on. Precede means go before.

Subject: english
Question or text: A short film will ___ the main film.
Explanation: Precede means go in front of or before.

Subject: english
Question or text: The shop made a ___ of £50.
Explanation: Profit is money made from selling things. A prophet foretells the future.

Subject: english
Question or text: The climbers began their ___ of the mountain.
Explanation: Ascent means going up. Assent means agreement.

Subject: english
Question or text: The head teacher gave her ___ to the plan.
Explanation: Assent means agreement.

Subject: english
Question or text: The plane began its ___ into London.
Explanation: Descent means going down. Dissent means disagreement.

Subject: english
Question or text: There was ___ among the players about the new rules.
Explanation: Dissent means disagreement.

Subject: english
Question or text: The rider fitted the ___ onto the horse.
Explanation: A bridle is the straps used to control a horse. Bridal is to do with a bride.

Subject: english
Question or text: The ___ shop sells wedding dresses.
Explanation: Bridal means to do with a bride.

Subject: english
Question or text: We need to ___ the length of these trousers.
Explanation: Alter means to change. An altar is a table in a church.

Subject: english
Question or text: The wizard made a ___ about the future king.
Explanation: Prophecy (with c) is the noun.

Subject: english
Question or text: The old woman claimed she could ___ the future.
Explanation: Prophesy (with s) is the verb.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which word is a synonym for "talk"?
Explanation: Synonyms have the same or similar meanings: talk and speak.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which word is a synonym for "old"?
Explanation: Old and elderly have similar meanings, so they are synonyms.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which word is a synonym for "begin"?
Explanation: Begin and start mean the same thing.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which word is an antonym of "ancient"?
Explanation: Antonyms have opposite meanings: ancient and modern.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which word is an antonym of "generous"?
Explanation: Generous and selfish are opposites, so they are antonyms.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which is the most formal way to say "find out"?
Choices: discover | check out | suss out | get
Explanation: In formal writing, "discover" replaces "find out".

Subject: english
Question or text: Which is the most formal way to say "ask for"?
Choices: request | go for | beg | shout for
Explanation: In formal writing, "request" replaces "ask for".

Subject: english
Question or text: Which is the most formal way to say "go in"?
Choices: enter | pop in | get in | nip in
Explanation: In formal writing, "enter" replaces "go in".

Subject: english
Question or text: Which is the most formal way to say "help"?
Choices: assist | give a hand | sort out | back up
Explanation: In formal writing, "assist" replaces "help".

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence is the most formal?
Choices: Pupils are requested to arrive by 9 a.m. | Get here by 9, OK? | Don't be late, guys! | Try and be in for 9.
Correct answer: Pupils are requested to arrive by 9 a.m.
Explanation: Formal writing avoids chatty words and uses vocabulary like "requested".

Subject: english
Question or text: In "The children will study the animals.", what is the subject?
Choices: The children | the animals | will study | study
Explanation: The subject is the "do-er" and normally comes just before the verb.

Subject: english
Question or text: In "Year 2 designed puppets.", what is the object?
Choices: puppets | Year 2 | designed | There is no object
Explanation: The object comes straight after the verb and shows what the verb acts on.

Subject: english
Question or text: In "Rula's mother went out.", what is the subject?
Choices: Rula's mother | out | went | went out
Explanation: The whole noun phrase "Rula's mother" is the subject: she did the going out.

Subject: english
Question or text: In "My brother kicked the ball over the fence.", what is the object?
Choices: the ball | My brother | the fence | kicked
Explanation: "The ball" comes straight after the verb and is what was kicked. "The fence" follows the preposition "over".

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence is written in the passive voice?
Choices: The window was broken by me. | I broke the window. | I am breaking the window. | I will break the window.
Correct answer: The window was broken by me.
Explanation: In a passive sentence the object becomes the subject, with "be" + past participle (was broken).

Subject: english
Question or text: Which is the passive version of "Our dog ate it."?
Choices: It was eaten by our dog. | Our dog has eaten it. | Our dog was eating it. | It ate our dog.
Correct answer: It was eaten by our dog.
Explanation: Passive: the object (it) becomes the subject, plus "was" + past participle (eaten).

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence is in the active voice?
Choices: The school arranged a visit. | A visit was arranged by the school. | A visit was arranged. | A visit was being arranged.
Explanation: In an active sentence the subject does the action: the school arranged.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence uses a question tag, a feature of informal speech?
Choices: He's your friend, isn't he? | Is he your friend? | He is your friend. | Your friend is here.
Explanation: A question tag is a short question added to the end of a statement: "isn't he?".

Subject: english
Question or text: Which adverbial shows a contrast between ideas?
Choices: On the other hand | As a consequence | Furthermore | Firstly
Explanation: "On the other hand" and "in contrast" link paragraphs by showing a difference.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence uses the subjunctive form?
Choices: If I were you, I would apologise. | If I was you, I would apologise. | I was sure I would apologise. | I am going to apologise.
Correct answer: If I were you, I would apologise.
Explanation: "If I were" is the subjunctive, used in formal writing.

Subject: english
Question or text: Choose the verb for formal writing: "The school requires that all pupils ___ honest."
Explanation: After "requires that", formal English uses the subjunctive "be".

Subject: english
Question or text: Which adverbial shows a result?
Choices: As a consequence | In contrast | On the other hand | However
Explanation: "As a consequence" shows that one thing happened because of another.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence uses ellipsis (leaving out words that are expected)?
Choices: I wanted to help but I couldn't. | I wanted to help and I helped. | I helped my friend with her homework. | My friend helped me with my homework.
Correct answer: I wanted to help but I couldn't.
Explanation: The word "help" is left out after "couldn't" because the reader can predict it.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which of these sentences is passive?
Choices: Our cat got run over by a bus. | He received a warning. | We had an accident. | A bus ran over our cat.
Correct answer: Our cat got run over by a bus.
Explanation: "Got run over" is passive: "get" + past participle. "Received" and "had" are just active past tense verbs.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence means you are inviting Grandma to eat with you?
Choices: Let's eat, Grandma! | Let's eat Grandma!
Explanation: The comma separates the person being spoken to. Without it, Grandma is on the menu!

Subject: english
Question or text: Which pair of punctuation marks can show parenthesis (extra information)?
Choices: Brackets | Full stops | Question marks | Apostrophes
Explanation: Brackets, dashes or commas can be used for parenthesis: My sister (who is 15) plays the drums.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence uses brackets correctly?
Choices: My sister (who is 15) plays the drums. | My sister (who is 15 plays) the drums. | (My sister) who is 15 plays the drums. | My sister who (is 15 plays the drums.)
Correct answer: My sister (who is 15) plays the drums.
Explanation: The brackets go around the extra information only. The sentence still makes sense without it.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence describes a shark that eats people?
Choices: A man-eating shark swam past. | A man eating shark swam past.
Explanation: The hyphen joins "man-eating" into one describing word. Without it, it sounds like a man is eating a shark!

Subject: english
Question or text: The sofa was worn out, so we had it ___.
Explanation: Re-cover (with a hyphen) means cover again. Recover means get better or get back.

Subject: english
Question or text: What does a hyphen help to avoid?
Choices: Ambiguity (a sentence having two meanings) | Long sentences | Capital letters | Speech
Explanation: Hyphens join words so the meaning is clear, like "man-eating shark".

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence uses a semi-colon correctly?
Choices: It's raining; I'm fed up. | It's; raining I'm fed up. | Because it's raining; I'm fed up. | It's raining I'm; fed up.
Explanation: A semi-colon joins two independent clauses (each could be a sentence on its own). "Because it's raining" is not independent.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which punctuation mark could join these two independent clauses: "The film was long ___ I nearly fell asleep."?
Choices: A semi-colon | A comma | An apostrophe | A hyphen
Explanation: A semi-colon (or a dash, or a colon) can mark the boundary between independent clauses. A comma alone cannot.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence uses a dash to join two independent clauses?
Choices: The shop was closed – we went home. | The – shop was closed we went home. | The shop – was closed we went home. | The shop was closed we – went home.
Correct answer: The shop was closed – we went home.
Explanation: The dash goes at the boundary between the two clauses.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
Choices: You will need the following: a pencil, a ruler and a rubber. | You will: need a pencil, a ruler and a rubber. | You will need a pencil: a ruler and a rubber. | You: will need a pencil, a ruler and a rubber.
Correct answer: You will need the following: a pencil, a ruler and a rubber.
Explanation: A colon can introduce a list after a complete clause.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence uses a colon correctly between two clauses?
Choices: I knew what had happened: the dog had eaten my homework. | I knew: what had happened the dog had eaten my homework. | I knew what: had happened the dog had eaten my homework. | I knew what had happened the dog: had eaten my homework.
Correct answer: I knew what had happened: the dog had eaten my homework.
Explanation: The colon comes at the boundary between the clauses. The second clause explains the first.

Subject: english
Question or text: What is a colon used for?
Choices: To introduce a list or an explanation | To show a question | To show possession | To end every sentence
Correct answer: To introduce a list or an explanation
Explanation: A colon (:) can introduce a list, or a clause that explains the first one.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence uses semi-colons correctly in a list?
Choices: We visited Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Madrid, Spain. | We visited Paris; France, Rome; Italy, and Madrid; Spain. | We visited; Paris, France, Rome, Italy, and Madrid, Spain. | We visited Paris France; Rome Italy and; Madrid Spain.
Correct answer: We visited Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Madrid, Spain.
Explanation: When list items already contain commas, semi-colons separate the items clearly.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which punctuation mark introduces a list?
Choices: A colon | A semi-colon | A hyphen | An apostrophe
Explanation: A colon introduces a list. Semi-colons can separate items within a list.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
Choices: I love summer; the days are long and warm. | I love summer, the days are long and warm. | I love summer the days are long and warm. | I love; summer the days are long and warm.
Correct answer: I love summer; the days are long and warm.
Explanation: Two independent clauses need a semi-colon (or a full stop), not just a comma.

Subject: english
Question or text: How many steps did Isla climb to reach the lamp room?
Explanation: The first paragraph says she climbed "the last of the hundred and twelve steps".

Subject: english
Question or text: Why had Isla's father gone to the mainland?
Choices: To fetch a new part for the lamp | To buy food for dinner | To get away from the storm | To visit Isla's school
Correct answer: To fetch a new part for the lamp
Explanation: Paragraph 2: "to fetch a new part for the lamp".

Subject: english
Question or text: "The sea hurled itself at the rocks." Which word is closest in meaning to "hurled"?
Explanation: To hurl something is to throw it hard. The writer makes the sea sound violent.

Subject: english
Question or text: Why did Isla's fingers tremble as she wound the mechanism?
Choices: She was nervous because she had never done it herself before. | She was angry with her father. | The brass handle was hot. | She was excited about going to the mainland.
Correct answer: She was nervous because she had never done it herself before.
Explanation: The text says she "had never been allowed to touch the brass handle herself", and her father was late in a storm: she is nervous.

Subject: english
Question or text: The windows were rattling "like loose teeth". What does this comparison suggest?
Choices: The windows were shaking so much they seemed ready to fall out. | The windows were white and shiny. | Isla had toothache. | The windows were small.
Correct answer: The windows were shaking so much they seemed ready to fall out.
Explanation: Loose teeth wobble and might fall out. The simile shows how hard the storm was shaking the windows.

Subject: english
Question or text: What does the horn sounding three short blasts most likely mean?
Choices: A boat out at sea has seen the light and is signalling back. | The storm is over. | Isla's father is cross with her. | The lamp has broken again.
Correct answer: A boat out at sea has seen the light and is signalling back.
Explanation: The horn answers the three sweeps of light, and Isla smiles for the first time: a boat, probably the ferry, has seen it.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence best sums up the whole passage?
Choices: When her father is late, Isla bravely lights the lamp on her own to guide a boat through the storm. | Isla climbs a lighthouse to watch a storm. | Isla's father teaches her how to light the lamp. | A ferry sinks in a storm.
Correct answer: When her father is late, Isla bravely lights the lamp on her own to guide a boat through the storm.
Explanation: A summary covers the whole passage, not just one part. The first choice only describes the first paragraph.

Subject: english
Question or text: Why does the writer include her father's promise, "Back by six", in paragraph 2?
Choices: To show he is late, which builds worry and explains why Isla must act. | To tell us what time the story starts. | To show that her father is always on time. | To describe the weather.
Correct answer: To show he is late, which builds worry and explains why Isla must act.
Explanation: Straight after the promise we learn it is half past seven. The promise makes his lateness, and the danger, clear.

Subject: english
Question or text: What is most likely to happen next?
Choices: Isla's father arrives safely on the ferry. | Isla switches off the lamp and goes to bed. | Isla swims to the mainland. | The lighthouse falls into the sea.
Correct answer: Isla's father arrives safely on the ferry.
Explanation: The horn answering the light, and Isla smiling, suggest the ferry has seen the light and will reach safety.

Subject: english
Question or text: Where did the fire start?
Choices: In a bakery on Pudding Lane | In St Paul's Cathedral | In Samuel Pepys's house | In a brick factory
Correct answer: In a bakery on Pudding Lane
Explanation: The first sentence says it "broke out in a bakery on Pudding Lane".

Subject: english
Question or text: How long did the fire last?
Choices: Four days | One night | Four weeks | Two days
Explanation: Paragraph 4: "four days later".

Subject: english
Question or text: "Their upper floors jutted out over the street." What does "jutted out" mean here?
Choices: stuck out | fell down | were painted | were hidden
Explanation: Jutted out means stuck out. The top floors stuck out so far that houses almost touched.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which of these helped the fire to spread quickly?
Choices: The houses were made of timber and built close together. | The houses were made of brick and stone. | It was raining heavily. | There were no streets.
Correct answer: The houses were made of timber and built close together.
Explanation: Paragraph 2: timber houses, narrow streets, a dry summer and a strong wind. Brick and stone came later, when London was rebuilt.

Subject: english
Question or text: In this text, what is a "firebreak"?
Choices: A gap that the fire cannot cross | A short rest for the people fighting the fire | A bucket of water | A type of gunpowder
Correct answer: A gap that the fire cannot cross
Explanation: The text explains it: "gaps, called firebreaks, that the fire could not cross". It isn't a break as in a rest.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which paragraph explains how people fought the fire?
Explanation: Paragraph 3 describes buckets, squirts and firebreaks.

Subject: english
Question or text: Why does the writer mention that the summer had been long and dry?
Choices: Dry wood burns easily, so it helps explain why the fire spread so fast. | To show it was a good summer holiday. | Because the fire happened in winter. | To show there was plenty of water.
Correct answer: Dry wood burns easily, so it helps explain why the fire spread so fast.
Explanation: The sentence is in the paragraph about why the fire spread. Dry timber catches fire more easily.

Subject: english
Question or text: Why does the text mention Samuel Pepys?
Choices: To explain how we know so much about the fire | Because he started the fire | Because he designed the new St Paul's | Because he was the baker
Correct answer: To explain how we know so much about the fire
Explanation: "We know a great deal about these days because of people like Samuel Pepys, who described them in his diary."

Subject: english
Question or text: How was London different after it was rebuilt?
Choices: More buildings were made of brick and stone instead of timber. | The streets were made even narrower. | St Paul's Cathedral was never rebuilt. | All the houses were made of wood again.
Correct answer: More buildings were made of brick and stone instead of timber.
Explanation: Compare paragraph 2 (timber houses) with paragraph 5 ("more buildings of brick and stone").

Subject: english
Question or text: Which heading would best sum up the last paragraph?
Choices: A new London | How the fire started | Pepys's diary | Fighting the flames
Explanation: The last paragraph is about rebuilding London and the new St Paul's.

Subject: english
Question or text: What is the green substance in leaves called?
Explanation: Paragraph 2: "a green substance called chlorophyll". Photosynthesis is the process, not the substance.

Subject: english
Question or text: When does the tree stop making chlorophyll?
Choices: When the days grow shorter and colder | In the middle of summer | When it rains | When new leaves grow in spring
Correct answer: When the days grow shorter and colder
Explanation: Paragraph 3: "As the days grow shorter and colder, the tree stops making chlorophyll".

Subject: english
Question or text: "Many trees put on a spectacular show." Which word means the same as "spectacular"?
Explanation: Spectacular means amazing and impressive to look at.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which colours were in the leaf all along?
Choices: Yellow and orange | Red and purple | Only green | Blue and brown
Explanation: Paragraph 3: "Yellow and orange colours, which were in the leaf all along". The red is made new in autumn.

Subject: english
Question or text: Why can't we see the yellow colours in summer?
Choices: The green chlorophyll hides them. | They haven't been made yet. | The sun bleaches them. | Leaves are yellow in summer.
Explanation: Paragraph 2: the green "hides everything else". The yellow is already there.

Subject: english
Question or text: The first paragraph ends with a question. Why?
Choices: To make the reader curious to find out the answer | Because the writer doesn't know the answer | To tell the reader to stop reading | To list the colours
Correct answer: To make the reader curious to find out the answer
Explanation: A question at the start of an information text hooks the reader; the rest of the text answers it.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence best sums up paragraph 4?
Choices: A sealing layer forms, the leaf falls, and the tree saves water and energy for winter. | Trees grow new leaves in spring. | Leaves turn yellow and orange. | Chlorophyll helps the tree make food.
Correct answer: A sealing layer forms, the leaf falls, and the tree saves water and energy for winter.
Explanation: The first choice covers the whole paragraph. "Trees grow new leaves in spring" is only its last few words.

Subject: english
Question or text: What is the difference between the yellow and the red colours in autumn leaves?
Choices: The yellow was there all along; the red is newly made in autumn by some trees. | Both are newly made in autumn. | The red was there all along; the yellow is new. | There is no difference.
Correct answer: The yellow was there all along; the red is newly made in autumn by some trees.
Explanation: Paragraph 3 says yellow and orange "were in the leaf all along", but some trees "make new red colours in autumn".

Subject: english
Question or text: What time does the station clock say?
Choices: Ten past nine | Nine o'clock | Ten to nine | Half past nine
Explanation: Line 1: "ten past nine".

Subject: english
Question or text: "A paper cup goes cartwheeling." What is the cup doing?
Choices: Tumbling over and over in the wind | Being carried by a passenger | Standing still on a bench | Being thrown into a bin
Correct answer: Tumbling over and over in the wind
Explanation: A cartwheel turns over and over. The cup is being blown along, turning as it goes.

Subject: english
Question or text: How does the speaker seem to feel on the platform at the start?
Choices: Cold and alone | Hot and tired | Excited and busy | Angry and loud
Explanation: The platform is "cold and bare" and the air is "empty": there is no one else there.

Subject: english
Question or text: The train's light is first "a silver thread". What does this suggest?
Choices: At first it is a thin, faint line of light far away. | The train is made of silver. | Someone is sewing. | The light is very close and bright.
Correct answer: At first it is a thin, faint line of light far away.
Explanation: A thread is thin. Far away, the light looks like a thin line that "begins to grow" as the train gets closer.

Subject: english
Question or text: "The doors sigh open." Why does the poet use the word "sigh"?
Choices: It makes the doors sound gentle and relieved, like a person breathing out. | Because the doors are broken. | To make the doors sound loud and scary. | Because the train is sad.
Correct answer: It makes the doors sound gentle and relieved, like a person breathing out.
Explanation: Giving the doors a human action (personification) makes the moment feel calm and welcoming.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which word in verse 2 compares the train to something in space?
Explanation: A comet is a bright object moving through space: the train's light moving through the dark.

Subject: english
Question or text: In the last verse, how have the speaker's feelings changed?
Choices: They now feel safe and warm instead of cold and lonely. | They feel more frightened than before. | They are angry that the train was late. | Their feelings have not changed.
Correct answer: They now feel safe and warm instead of cold and lonely.
Explanation: Verse 1 is "cold and bare"; verse 3 is "warm and bright" and "safe inside".

Subject: english
Question or text: How is the poem organised?
Choices: It follows the journey in order: waiting, the train arriving, then riding home. | It starts at home and goes back in time. | Each verse is about a different person. | It is a list of train times.
Correct answer: It follows the journey in order: waiting, the train arriving, then riding home.
Explanation: Verse 1 waits on the platform, verse 2 sees the train coming, verse 3 is on board heading home.

Subject: english
Question or text: "I'm swallowed, safe inside." Why is "swallowed" a good choice of word?
Choices: It makes the train seem like a creature taking the speaker in, and "safe" shows this feels comforting. | It shows the speaker is eating on the train. | It shows the train is dangerous. | It means the speaker is very small.
Correct answer: It makes the train seem like a creature taking the speaker in, and "safe" shows this feels comforting.
Explanation: Swallowed makes the train seem alive, but "safe" tells us the feeling is comfort, not fear.

Subject: english
Question or text: When does the Reading Club meet?
Choices: Every Saturday | Every Sunday | After school on Fridays | Once a year
Explanation: Paragraph 2: "Every Saturday, the Reading Club…".

Subject: english
Question or text: Why might the council close the library?
Choices: To save money | Because it is too noisy | Because nobody uses it | Because it needs new books
Explanation: Paragraph 1: "the council may close it next year to save money".

Subject: english
Question or text: "This would be a serious mistake." Which word could replace "serious" without changing the meaning?
Explanation: Here "serious" means important or big. It isn't about someone being solemn.

Subject: english
Question or text: What is the main purpose of this letter?
Choices: To persuade the councillor to keep the library open | To tell a story about a library | To complain about her brother | To explain how to use a computer
Correct answer: To persuade the councillor to keep the library open
Explanation: The first line says so: "I am writing to ask you to keep Brookfield Library open."

Subject: english
Question or text: Why does Amara use the words "Firstly" and "Secondly"?
Choices: To organise her reasons clearly, one after another | To show her first reason is less important | To show she is unsure | To count the books
Correct answer: To organise her reasons clearly, one after another
Explanation: Words like "firstly" and "secondly" signpost each new reason in a persuasive text.

Subject: english
Question or text: Why does Amara mention her neighbour who is eighty-three?
Choices: As an example of someone who needs the librarians' help with technology | To show her neighbour works at the library | Because her neighbour wants the library to close | To show that only older people use the library
Correct answer: As an example of someone who needs the librarians' help with technology
Explanation: The neighbour is her example of someone who "finds technology difficult" and is helped by the librarians.

Subject: english
Question or text: "Where else would we go?" Why does Amara ask this question?
Choices: To make the reader realise the children would have nowhere else to meet | Because she wants the councillor to reply with a place | Because she is lost | To change the subject
Correct answer: To make the reader realise the children would have nowhere else to meet
Explanation: It's a rhetorical question: she doesn't expect an answer. It makes the reader think about what would be lost.

Subject: english
Question or text: Which sentence best sums up Amara's argument?
Choices: The library helps the whole community, so it should stay open. | Everything is online now, so libraries are not needed. | Her brother likes revising in quiet places. | Councillors should visit more buildings.
Correct answer: The library helps the whole community, so it should stay open.
Explanation: Her reasons (friends, homework, computers, help) all support keeping it open. The "everything is online" view is the one she argues against.

Subject: english
Question or text: How does Amara deal with the view that "everything is online now"?
Choices: She mentions it, then gives reasons against it. | She agrees with it completely. | She ignores it. | She says computers should be banned.
Correct answer: She mentions it, then gives reasons against it.
Explanation: "Some people say… However…": she answers the other side's point, which makes her argument stronger.

Subject: english
Question or text: Why does Amara end with "I am sure you will agree"?
Choices: It politely assumes the councillor shares her view, which makes it harder to disagree. | It shows she is unsure. | It is a question the councillor must answer. | It lists her reasons.
Correct answer: It politely assumes the councillor shares her view, which makes it harder to disagree.
Explanation: Sounding confident that the reader agrees is a persuasive technique.

Subject: maths

Question or text:
The Keeper's Daughter (Story)

The storm had been building all afternoon. By the time Isla climbed the last of the hundred and twelve steps, the windows of the lamp room were rattling in their frames like loose teeth. Below her, the sea hurled itself at the rocks, then drew back, gathering strength for the next attack.

Her father had gone to the mainland that morning to fetch a new part for the lamp. "Back by six," he had promised, ruffling her hair. It was now half past seven, and the little ferry had not returned.

Isla knew what she had to do. She had watched her father light the great lamp a thousand times, though she had never been allowed to touch the brass handle herself. Her fingers trembled as she wound the mechanism, counting each turn under her breath exactly as he did: "Twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three."

With a low hum, the lamp began to turn. A beam of white light swept across the water, once, twice, three times. Somewhere out in the darkness, a horn sounded: three short blasts. Isla pressed her face to the cold glass and, for the first time that evening, she smiled.

Question or text:
The Great Fire of London (Information)

In the early hours of Sunday 2 September 1666, a fire broke out in a bakery on Pudding Lane in the City of London. The baker, Thomas Farriner, had gone to bed believing his oven was safe. Within hours, the flames had spread to the houses around it.

At the time, London's streets were narrow and crowded. Most houses were built from timber, and their upper floors jutted out over the street, so that buildings on opposite sides almost touched. The summer had been long and dry, and a strong wind from the east blew the fire from one street to the next.

People tried to stop the fire with leather buckets of water and hand-held squirts, but these were no match for the blaze. Eventually, houses were pulled down or blown up with gunpowder to create gaps, called firebreaks, that the fire could not cross.

By the time the fire was put out, four days later, much of the City lay in ruins, including the old St Paul's Cathedral. We know a great deal about these days because of people like Samuel Pepys, who described them in his diary.

London was rebuilt, this time with more buildings of brick and stone. The architect Christopher Wren designed a new St Paul's Cathedral, which still stands today.

Question or text:
Why Do Leaves Change Colour? (Information)

Every autumn, many trees in Britain put on a spectacular show. Leaves that were green all summer turn yellow, orange, red and brown before falling to the ground. But where do these colours come from?

During spring and summer, leaves are packed with a green substance called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll allows the tree to capture energy from sunlight and use it to make food from water and carbon dioxide. This process is called photosynthesis. There is so much chlorophyll in a leaf that its green colour hides everything else.

As the days grow shorter and colder, the tree stops making chlorophyll, and the green slowly breaks down. Yellow and orange colours, which were in the leaf all along, can now be seen. Some trees, such as certain maples, also make new red colours in autumn.

Finally, a layer of special cells forms where each leaf joins its twig. This seals the leaf off, and before long it drops. By losing their leaves, trees save water and energy through the winter, ready to grow new leaves in spring.

Question or text:
The Last Train Home (Poem)

The station clock says ten past nine,
the platform's cold and bare;
a paper cup goes cartwheeling
through empty evening air.

Then, far away, a silver thread
of light begins to grow;
it slides along the sleeping rails,
a comet, low and slow.

The doors sigh open, warm and bright;
I'm swallowed, safe inside.
The dark rolls past like velvet sea,
and home is one more ride.

Question or text:
Save Our Library! (Letter)

Dear Councillor Patel,

I am writing to ask you to keep Brookfield Library open. I have heard that the council may close it next year to save money, and I believe this would be a serious mistake.

Firstly, the library is much more than a building full of books. Every Saturday, the Reading Club brings together children from different schools, and many of us have made friends there. Where else would we go?

Secondly, not every family can afford to buy books or has a quiet place to do homework. The library gives everyone the same chance, whatever their background. My older brother did all his revision there because our flat is too noisy.

Some people say that everything is online now, so libraries are no longer needed. However, the library's computers are free to use, and the librarians help people who find technology difficult, such as my neighbour, who is eighty-three.

Please visit the library on a Saturday morning and see for yourself how important it is. I am sure you will agree that closing it would be a loss for the whole community.

Yours sincerely,
Amara Okafor (aged 11)
